name: Ben Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right. I'm not much of a talker, but I'll give it a go.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in claims at a farmers' mutual insurer, in a brick office by the cattle market in our market town. Farmers ring in when a barn roof blows off, a tractor's stolen, or they lose sheep to dogs. I take the details, check the policy, book the loss adjuster and keep the file moving. A lot of our members still post in handwritten forms, and some of them only want to speak to someone who knows what a baler is.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that I know the people. My dad farmed until he sold the herd, so half the members knew him. What wears me out is the screen work, and the new online claim form the head office keeps pushing, which our members hate. I'm engaged to Ruth, who cooks at the primary school, and we're getting married at our chapel next summer. Money's tight: about three weeks saved, and most of that is meant for the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Good. That sounds about right to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers want a person on the phone, not a computer, and that's not changing. I don't post online much, but I'd say it at chapel and at the market. I'd say the head office should spend less on gadgets and more on paying the people who keep the members happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think even the bit of automation would hit the typing side of my job. If the system reads the online forms, they'd need fewer of us in the office. I don't think they'd sack me, because members ask for me by name, but I'd not get a raise. And the wedding's already costing more than we've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, keep the members happy, and keep my head down. I'd ask my uncle Geoff if he needs help at lambing time for some extra cash. And Ruth and I would cut the wedding list from a hundred and twenty to eighty, which her mum won't like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's mostly the wedding money. The job feels steady enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI tools at all. Would you ever?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not if I can help it. I don't trust a computer to understand a farmer whose barn's just come down in a storm. Old Mr Pryce (a farmer we insure) rang last month in tears about his roof, and he needed a person, not a menu.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Cutting the wedding list. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, at first. Ruth's mum has been planning it since Ruth was ten. But Ruth's sensible, and she'd rather start married life without a loan. We'd keep the chapel and the hall, just fewer cousins.

say: Farmers want **a person** on the phone, not a computer, and that won't change.
Head office should spend **less on gadgets** and more on the people who serve members.
think: Even a little automation would hit the **typing side** of his claims work.
He expects to keep the job, but with **no raise** while wedding costs rise.
do: Carry on serving members and **keep his head down** at the office.
Help his **uncle Geoff** at lambing time for extra cash.
Cut the **wedding list** from a hundred and twenty to eighty.
feel: Reassured that the **job feels steady** enough.
S0.quote: Old Mr Pryce (a farmer we insure) rang last month in tears about his roof, and he needed a person, not a menu.
fieldNote: Ben's identity is tied to **farming roots** and personal service.
He refuses AI tools out of **distrust**, not ignorance.
The **wedding cost** is his main pressure in this picture.
Family, like **uncle Geoff**, is his first source of extra income.

steps.text: Keep handling farm claims by phone for members
Help uncle Geoff at lambing time for extra cash
Cut the wedding guest list from 120 to 80

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking, booking, answering customers. That's my day, more or less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the mutual should remember it belongs to its members, and farmers didn't ask for a chatbot. I'd say it to the manager and at the members' meeting. I wouldn't be marching, but I'd speak up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the office goes from nine of us to maybe four. The online form would read the claims, and the adjusters would get booked automatically. Members who ask for me might keep me on for a bit, but I'm average and I don't use the tools, so I'd be at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask uncle Geoff if he'd take me on part-time at the farm, maybe two days a week, and learn the stock work properly. I'd keep the office job as long as they'd have me. Ruth and I would move the wedding to a smaller do and put the rest into savings. I'd go to the members' meeting and speak up for keeping local staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's not the end of the world, but it feels like the ground's going soft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Farm work instead of office work. Is that a step back for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not in my head. My dad worked the land his whole life, and I went into an office because there was no money in milk. If the office goes, going back to the land isn't a failure for a farmer's son like me. It's just home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Margaret, who's been there thirty years and knows every family in the county. She's sixty-one and she's not learning a new system. If they let her go, the members would lose more than they know.

say: The mutual belongs to **its members**, and farmers didn't ask for a chatbot.
He'd speak up at the **members' meeting** rather than march.
think: The office could shrink from **nine to four** once claims are read automatically.
As an average clerk who avoids AI tools, he'd be **at risk**.
do: Ask uncle Geoff for **two days a week** of farm work.
Keep the **office job** as long as the mutual keeps him.
Move the wedding to a **smaller do** and save the rest.
feel: Steadied by knowing the **land** is there.
S1.quote: If the office goes, going back to the land isn't a failure for a farmer's son like me.
fieldNote: Ben sees **farm work** as a return home, not a step down.
He worries about **Margaret (his colleague)**, who knows every family.
His resistance to AI tools leaves him **exposed** in office cuts.
He uses the **members' meeting** rather than protests.

steps.text: Work two days a week on uncle Geoff's farm
Stay in the claims office as long as possible
Hold a smaller wedding and save the difference
Speak up for local staff at the members' meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's daft. That's before we've even had a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong for a few big companies to turn everything upside down that fast. Families and churches will have to hold people together. I'd say government should slow it down, but I wouldn't trust them to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my office job's gone within a year. Everything I do is reading and checking, and an AGI would do it better. Farm work is hands-on, so maybe I've got until 2031, but even then, robots on farms will come. I honestly don't know what I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to uncle Geoff straight away and ask for full-time work, even if it's low pay. We'd cancel the big wedding and get married quietly at chapel. I'd lean on the church for help if things got bad, and we'd move in with Ruth's mum to save rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. I don't like change, and this is too much too fast. I'd feel like the ground had gone from under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever use AI tools in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. If they're replacing me, I'm not helping them. I'd rather put my hands in the soil and hope for the best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ruth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ruth (my fiancée) we'd be okay, but I'd not believe it. She'd say God has a plan. I'd hope she's right.

say: It's wrong for **a few big companies** to turn everything upside down so fast.
**Families and churches** will have to hold people together through it.
think: His office job is **gone within a year**, since it's all reading and checking.
Farm work buys time until **about 2031**, but he has no real plan.
do: Ask uncle Geoff for **full-time farm work**, even at low pay.
Cancel the big wedding and marry **quietly at chapel**.
Move in with **Ruth's mum** and lean on the church.
feel: **Panicked**, with too much change too fast.
Like the **ground's gone** from under him.
S2.quote: I'd tell Ruth (my fiancée) we'd be okay, but I'd not believe it.
fieldNote: Ben's resistance turns into **panic** under fast change.
He'd refuse AI tools on **principle**.
His fallback is **family and church**, not government.
He knows farm work only **delays** the robots.

steps.text: Ask uncle Geoff for full-time farm work
Marry quietly at chapel instead of a big wedding
Move in with Ruth's mum to save rent
Lean on the chapel community for help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast, but at least there's a bit of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families should start preparing now. Learn a trade, keep land in the family, help each other out. I'd say it at chapel and at the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the office job goes around 2030. I'd work part-time on Geoff's farm before then and learn stock work properly. That gives me until about 2034, when robots might come to farms too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do two days a week at the farm next year and keep the office job. We'd have a small wedding and save what we can. I'd look at a short course in farm machinery repair at the agricultural college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but not panicked. There's time to get some skills, but it's still fast for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why machinery repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tractors break, and someone has to fix them, even if robots come. Someone has to keep the robots running too, and I'd rather be that someone than nobody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take help from the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I had to. I'd rather earn it. But if it came to it, I'd swallow my pride for Ruth's sake.

say: Families should **start preparing now** by learning trades.
Keep **land in the family** and help each other out.
think: The office job goes **around 2030**, he thinks.
Farm work would last until **about 2034**, when robots might reach farms.
do: Work **two days a week** at the farm next year.
Keep the **office job** and save what he can.
Take a **machinery repair** course at the agricultural college.
feel: Still finds it **too fast** for someone like him.
S3.quote: Tractors break, and someone has to fix them, even if robots come.
fieldNote: Ben sees **repair skills** as a lasting role.
He'd take state help only **reluctantly**.
Family land and **Geoff's farm** anchor his plans.
His mood stays **alarmed** because he's slow to change.

steps.text: Work two days a week on uncle Geoff's farm
Take a farm machinery repair course at the college
Hold a small wedding and save the rest

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Okay. That's more like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for families to plan. Apprenticeships, not handouts. I'd say young people should learn real skills now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the office job lasts until around 2033. By then I'd have done machinery repair training and could work with Geoff full-time. That would last until about 2039, maybe longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the machinery course in two years, after the wedding. I'd keep the office job and help on the farm at weekends. We'd save for a house deposit, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. Ten years is enough time for me to change, even if I'm slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about having children in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still have them. I'd just want them to learn with their hands as well as their heads. My dad taught me to fix a fence before I could read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the mutual?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honesty. Tell us what's coming and help us train for something. Don't just send an email one day saying we're done.

say: Ten years is enough time for **families to plan** properly.
**Apprenticeships, not handouts**, should help young people learn real skills.
think: The office job could last until **around 2033**.
**Machinery repair** with Geoff would last until about 2039, maybe longer.
do: Start the **machinery course** in two years, after the wedding.
Keep the office job and help on the **farm at weekends**.
feel: Confident that ten years is **enough time** to change slowly.
S4.quote: My dad taught me to fix a fence before I could read.
fieldNote: Ten years makes Ben's slow approach **workable**.
He still sees **hands-on work** as the safest path.
He values **honesty** from his employer.
Family plans continue, with **children** still wanted.

steps.text: Start the machinery repair course after the wedding
Keep the claims job and help on the farm at weekends
Save slowly for a house deposit with Ruth

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years is no time at all for someone like me. What would help is a proper apprenticeship and honest notice from the mutual.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about faith and community. Out here in farming country, faith and community are what hold people together when work goes.

headlineQuote: Out here in farming country, faith and community are what hold people together when work goes.
portrait: Ben is a **27-year-old claims clerk** at a farmers' mutual in a market town.
He's a **farmer's son**, engaged to Ruth, with about three weeks saved for the wedding.
He **never uses AI** and distrusts it for farm members.
His fallback is **uncle Geoff's farm** and later machinery repair.
Fast change leaves him **panicked**, while ten years feels workable.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is no time for someone like him.
whatWouldHelp: A proper **apprenticeship** and honest notice from the mutual.
